name: Chain
how: With a loop on the hook, yarn over and draw the yarn through the loop on the hook.
use: Foundations, turning chains, spaces, loops and bridges in lace.
tip: Chain loosely or with a hook one size larger if your first row pulls in.
mistake: Counting the loop on the hook as a chain. It never counts.

name: Slip stitch
how: Insert hook into the stitch, yarn over, draw through the stitch and the loop on the hook in one motion.
use: Joining rounds, moving across stitches without height, seams, surface embroidery, slip-stitch crochet fabric.
tip: Worked in the back loop row after row, slip stitches make a very stretchy ribbing.
mistake: Pulling the slip stitch so tight that the next row cannot be worked into it.

name: Single crochet
h: About 1 chain tall; ch 1 to turn (not counted)
how: Insert hook, yarn over, draw up a loop (2 loops on hook); yarn over, draw through both loops.
use: Dense, firm fabric: amigurumi, bags, edgings, tapestry.
tip: The US ‘single’ is the UK ‘double’. Check which terms a pattern uses before starting.
mistake: Losing a stitch at the row ends: skipping the last stitch, or working into a turning chain that the pattern says does not count.

name: Half double crochet
h: About 2 chains tall; ch 1 or 2 to turn
how: Yarn over, insert hook, yarn over and draw up a loop (3 loops); yarn over, draw through all 3 loops.
use: Warm, quick fabric with a soft texture; hats, blankets, scarves.
tip: Behind every hdc is a third loop (back bar) you can work into for knit-look ribbing.
mistake: Losing the last stitch of the row: the turning chain sits beside it and hides it.

name: Double crochet
h: About 3 chains tall; ch 3 often counts as the first dc
how: Yarn over, insert, yarn over and draw up a loop (3 loops); [yarn over, draw through 2 loops] twice.
use: Granny squares, shells, filet, quick drapey fabric.
tip: If ch 3 counts as a stitch, work the last stitch of the next row into its top chain.
mistake: Forgetting whether the ch 3 counts as a stitch, which adds or loses one at every edge.

name: Treble crochet
h: About 4 chains tall; ch 4 to turn
how: Yarn over twice, insert, yarn over and draw up a loop (4 loops); [yarn over, draw through 2] three times.
use: Lace, open fabric, tall spike and post designs.
tip: Keep the first two wraps snug on the shaft; loose wraps make sloppy tall stitches.
mistake: Losing a stitch at the row ends: skipping the last stitch, or working into a turning chain that the pattern says does not count.

name: Double treble crochet
how: Yarn over 3 times, insert, yarn over and draw up a loop (5 loops); [yarn over, draw through 2] four times.
use: Very open lace, bridging long distances in motifs.
tip: Tall stitches use a lot of yarn per stitch but build height quickly.
mistake: Losing a stitch at the row ends: skipping the last stitch, or working into a turning chain that the pattern says does not count.

name: Triple treble crochet
how: Yarn over 4 times, insert, draw up a loop (6 loops); [yarn over, draw through 2] five times.
use: Rare; used for dramatic lace and long sun-ray motifs.
tip: Count wraps aloud. One extra wrap changes the stitch.
mistake: Losing a stitch at the row ends: skipping the last stitch, or working into a turning chain that the pattern says does not count.

name: Extended single crochet
how: Insert, yarn over, draw up a loop (2 loops); yarn over, draw through 1 loop (a chain at the base); yarn over, draw through 2 loops.
use: Softer, more flexible fabric than sc; good for drapey garments.
tip: Abbreviations for extended stitches vary between designers; always check the pattern key.
mistake: Switching between the extended and standard versions partway through, which changes the fabric height.

name: Extended double crochet
how: Yarn over, insert, draw up a loop (3 loops); yarn over, draw through 1 loop; [yarn over, draw through 2] twice.
use: Taller, looser columns.
tip: Use when dc looks too stiff but tr is too open.
mistake: Switching between the extended and standard versions partway through, which changes the fabric height.

name: Foundation single crochet
h: A chain and a sc made together
how: Ch 2, insert in 2nd ch from hook, draw up a loop, yarn over and draw through 1 (this is the ‘chain’), yarn over and draw through 2 (the sc). For each next stitch, insert into the ‘chain’ of the previous stitch and repeat.
use: Stretchy starting edges that match the first row exactly; no long foundation chain to count.
tip: Excellent for hat brims and necklines that must stretch.
mistake: Working too tightly, so the first row will not stretch to match the fabric above it.

name: Foundation double crochet
how: Ch 4, yarn over, insert in 4th ch from hook, draw up a loop, yarn over and draw through 1 (chain), [yarn over, draw through 2] twice. For later stitches, yarn over, insert into the chain of the previous stitch and repeat.
use: Stretchy, quick foundation rows for dc fabric.
tip: Mark the ‘chain’ part of the first few stitches until you can see it easily.
mistake: Working too tightly, so the first row will not stretch to match the fabric above it.

name: Standing single crochet
how: Place a slip knot of the new yarn on the hook, insert into the stitch, yarn over, draw up a loop, yarn over and draw through both loops.
use: Starting a new color mid-round without a slip stitch and chain.
tip: Gives granny squares and motifs a cleaner round start.
mistake: Working too tightly, so the first row will not stretch to match the fabric above it.

name: Back loop only
how: Insert the hook under only the back (far) loop of the stitch’s top V, then complete the stitch as usual.
use: Ribbing, ridges, stretchy bands, places to attach later rounds.
tip: BLO single crochet worked in rows produces a horizontal rib that stretches widthwise; turn it sideways for cuffs.
mistake: Changing which loop or space you work into from row to row, so the texture shifts.

name: Front loop only
how: Insert the hook under only the front (near) loop of the top V, then complete the stitch.
use: Surface texture; leaving a free back loop for later stitches or attaching ruffles.
tip: The unused loops can host a second fabric layer—this is how many dimensional flowers are built.
mistake: Changing which loop or space you work into from row to row, so the texture shifts.

name: Third-loop half double crochet
how: Turn the work slightly to see the horizontal bar below the top V on the back of the hdc; insert under that bar only and work an hdc.
use: Knit-look ribbing (sometimes called camel stitch) on hats and cuffs.
tip: Work it from the right side in rounds for a consistent look.
mistake: Changing which loop or space you work into from row to row, so the texture shifts.

name: Center single crochet
how: Insert the hook between the two vertical legs of the stitch below (into the center of the V, through the fabric), then complete a sc.
use: Dense, knit-look fabric; straighter vertical lines in tapestry worked in rounds.
tip: Insertion is tight: use a pointed hook and a slightly larger size.
mistake: Changing which loop or space you work into from row to row, so the texture shifts.

name: Front post double crochet
how: Yarn over, insert the hook from front to back to front around the post of the indicated stitch (hook in front of the post), yarn over, draw up a loop, [yarn over, draw through 2] twice.
use: Ribbing, cables, basketweave, raised columns.
tip: Post stitches use more yarn and pull fabric narrower; swatch the full pattern.
mult: Set by the rib or cable pattern
mistake: Inserting into the top of the stitch instead of around the post, or pulling the yarn over too tight for the extra height.

name: Back post double crochet
h: About dc height, recessed on the facing side
how: Yarn over, insert the hook from back to front to back around the post (hook behind the post), yarn over, draw up a loop, [yarn over, draw through 2] twice.
use: Pairs with FPdc for ribbing; makes a raised ridge on the opposite face.
tip: A BPdc on a wrong-side row raises the column on the right side.
mult: Set by the rib or cable pattern
mistake: Inserting into the top of the stitch instead of around the post, or pulling the yarn over too tight for the extra height.

name: Front post single crochet
how: Insert around the post from the front, yarn over, draw up a loop, yarn over, draw through 2.
use: Surface ridges, outlines, reinforcing rows.
tip: Good for adding a raised line around a hat brim boundary.
mult: Set by the rib or cable pattern
mistake: Inserting into the top of the stitch instead of around the post, or pulling the yarn over too tight for the extra height.

name: Front post treble crochet
how: Yarn over twice, insert around the post from the front, draw up a loop, [yarn over, draw through 2] three times.
use: Cables crossing over several rows, raised zigzags.
tip: Tall post stitches often reach down two rows to the post of a stitch below.
mult: Set by the rib or cable pattern
mistake: Inserting into the top of the stitch instead of around the post, or pulling the yarn over too tight for the extra height.

name: Single crochet two together
how: [Insert in next st, yarn over, draw up a loop] twice (3 loops), yarn over, draw through all 3.
use: Decreasing one stitch in sc fabric.
tip: For invisible decreases in amigurumi, use the front-loop version below.
mistake: Losing track of how many stitches the decrease removes; the count should drop by exactly the number the pattern states.

name: Invisible decrease
how: Insert the hook in the front loop of the next stitch and the front loop of the following stitch (3 loops on hook), yarn over, draw through the 2 front loops, yarn over, draw through the remaining 2.
use: Smooth decreases on the right side of amigurumi worked in spirals.
tip: Works because it takes only front loops; the back loops stay behind and the surface stays smooth.
mistake: Inserting under both loops by habit; only the front loops are used.

name: Single crochet three together
how: [Insert in next st, yarn over, draw up a loop] three times (4 loops), yarn over, draw through all 4.
use: Double decreases, mitered corners, the valleys of a ripple.
tip: Center the decrease over the stitch you want to point to.
mistake: Losing track of how many stitches the decrease removes; the count should drop by exactly the number the pattern states.

name: Half double crochet two together
how: [Yarn over, insert in next st, draw up a loop] twice (5 loops), yarn over, draw through all 5.
use: Decreases in hdc fabric.
tip: Some designers draw through 3 then 3; follow the pattern key if it differs.
mistake: Losing track of how many stitches the decrease removes; the count should drop by exactly the number the pattern states.

name: Double crochet two together
how: [Yarn over, insert in next st, draw up a loop, yarn over, draw through 2] twice (3 loops), yarn over, draw through all 3.
use: Decreases in dc fabric; tops of shaped lace.
tip: The same motion worked all in one stitch makes a cluster instead of a decrease.
mistake: Losing track of how many stitches the decrease removes; the count should drop by exactly the number the pattern states.

name: Double crochet three together
how: [Yarn over, insert in next st, draw up a loop, yarn over, draw through 2] three times (4 loops), yarn over, draw through all 4.
use: Ripple valleys, star centers.
tip: Mark the center stitch of the three so ripples stay aligned.
mistake: Losing track of how many stitches the decrease removes; the count should drop by exactly the number the pattern states.

name: Increase
how: Work two stitches into the same stitch.
use: Circles, spheres, shaping.
tip: Spread increases evenly and stagger them from round to round.
mistake: Not counting after increase rounds, so the piece cups (too few) or ruffles (too many).

name: V-stitch
how: (Dc, ch 1, dc) in the same stitch or space. On the next row, work the next V-st into the ch-1 space of the V below.
use: Light, quick openwork for shawls and blankets.
tip: Definitions vary: some V-stitches use ch 2 or hdc. Read the key.
mistake: Placing the group in the wrong stitch or space; every repeat after it shifts.

name: Shell
how: Work several stitches (commonly 5 dc) into the same stitch or space, usually with skipped stitches on each side to keep the count balanced.
use: Edgings, scallops, lace, blankets.
tip: A 5-dc shell between ‘skip 2’ on each side keeps the row count steady over a 6-stitch repeat.
mult: Ch a multiple of 6 + 2 (classic shell rows)
mistake: Placing the group in the wrong stitch or space; every repeat after it shifts.

name: Fan
how: A large shell, often with chains between the stitches, such as (dc, ch 1) 4 times, dc in the same space.
use: Lacy borders and pineapple-style motifs.
tip: Count spaces as well as stitches in fans.
mistake: Placing the group in the wrong stitch or space; every repeat after it shifts.

name: Cluster
how: [Yarn over, insert in the stitch, draw up a loop, yarn over, draw through 2] three times in the same stitch (4 loops), yarn over, draw through all 4.
use: Gentle texture, lace motifs, granny-style rounds.
tip: Patterns define clusters differently; count of stitches and where they are worked must be stated.
mistake: Placing the group in the wrong stitch or space; every repeat after it shifts.

name: Bobble
how: [Yarn over, insert in same st, draw up a loop, yarn over, draw through 2] five times (6 loops), yarn over, draw through all 6. Usually worked on a wrong-side row between sc so it pops to the right side.
use: Bold 3-D texture on blankets, pillows, hats.
tip: Bobbles eat yarn: a bobble blanket uses much more than a plain one.
mistake: Placing the group in the wrong stitch or space; every repeat after it shifts.

name: Puff stitch
how: [Yarn over, insert in same st, draw up a loop to the height of the row] three or more times (7 loops for three draw-ups), yarn over, draw through all loops; often closed with ch 1.
use: Soft, plump texture; flowers; baby blankets.
tip: Pull each loop to the same height before drawing through, or the puff looks lopsided.
mistake: Pulling the loops up to uneven heights, so the puff will not close neatly.

name: Popcorn
how: Work 5 dc in the same stitch. Remove the hook from the loop, insert it from front to back into the top of the first dc of the group, put the dropped loop back on the hook and draw it through; ch 1 to close if the pattern says so.
use: Crisp, round dimensional bumps.
tip: Insert from the back instead to push the popcorn to the other side.
mistake: Forgetting to drop the loop and pick it up through the first stitch, which makes a bobble-like group instead.

name: Spike stitch
how: Insert the hook into the indicated stitch one or more rows below, draw up a loop to the height of the current row, and finish as a sc.
use: Color patterns and checks without carrying yarn.
tip: Draw the loop up long enough so the fabric does not pucker.
mistake: Losing the repeat at the row edges; count the multiple on the first row and check it every few rows.

name: Crossed double crochet
how: Skip 1 st, dc in the next st, then dc in the skipped st, working in front of (or around) the first dc.
use: Woven, lattice-like rows.
tip: Work the crossing stitch in front for a raised cross, behind for a flatter one.
mistake: Losing the repeat at the row edges; count the multiple on the first row and check it every few rows.

name: Surface slip stitch
how: Hold the yarn behind the fabric; insert the hook from front to back through the fabric, draw up a loop and through the loop on the hook; continue along the line to embroider.
use: Lines, plaids, outlines, lettering on finished fabric.
tip: Keep surface stitches the same length as the fabric’s stitches to avoid puckering.
mult: Set by the stitch pattern; check your pattern
mistake: Losing the repeat at the row edges; count the multiple on the first row and check it every few rows.

name: Reverse single crochet
how: Working from left to right (right-handed): insert in the next stitch to the right, draw up a loop, yarn over and draw through both loops.
use: A corded, twisted edge for blankets and cuffs.
tip: It feels awkward because the hook moves ‘backward’. Keep loops loose.
mistake: Working too many or too few stitches along row ends, so the edge ruffles or pulls in.

name: Picot
how: Ch 3 (or as stated), sl st in the third chain from the hook (or into the top of the last stitch, depending on the pattern).
use: Dainty edges, doilies, Irish crochet.
tip: Decide whether the sl st goes into the chain or into the stitch below; patterns differ.
mistake: Working too many or too few stitches along row ends, so the edge ruffles or pulls in.

name: Moss stitch (linen / granite stitch)
how: Foundation of an even number of chains. Row 1: sc in 4th ch from hook, *ch 1, skip 1 ch, sc in next ch; rep. Later rows: work sc into each ch-1 space with ch 1 between, skipping the sc stitches.
use: Woven-look fabric with drape: scarves, wraps, dishcloths.
tip: Sc go into spaces, not into stitches—this is what makes it lie flat and woven.
mistake: Losing the repeat at the row edges; count the multiple on the first row and check it every few rows.

name: Griddle stitch
how: Alternate sc and dc across the row. On the next row, work sc into dc and dc into sc.
use: Bumpy, dense texture for washcloths and blankets.
tip: Even stitch counts keep the alternation clean.
mistake: Losing the repeat at the row edges; count the multiple on the first row and check it every few rows.

name: Lemon peel stitch
how: Alternate sc and dc across; on following rows work sc in sc and dc in dc, offsetting so the texture shifts. Construction varies by designer.
use: Pebbled texture.
tip: Different sources describe this stitch with different offsets—use the version in your pattern.
mult: Set by the stitch pattern; check your pattern
mistake: Losing the repeat at the row edges; count the multiple on the first row and check it every few rows.

name: Suzette stitch
how: *(Sc, dc) in the same stitch, skip the next stitch; rep. On later rows, work the (sc, dc) pair into each sc of the previous row.
use: Dense, slightly ridged fabric with good drape.
tip: Counts are in pairs; mark every tenth pair.
mistake: Losing the repeat at the row edges; count the multiple on the first row and check it every few rows.

name: Herringbone half double crochet
how: Yarn over, insert, draw the loop through the stitch AND through the first loop on the hook (2 loops), yarn over, draw through both.
use: A slanting, woven-look fabric.
tip: Because the first loop is pulled through, the stitch slants; alternate directions for chevrons.
mistake: Losing the repeat at the row edges; count the multiple on the first row and check it every few rows.

name: Waffle stitch
how: Over a dc base, alternate dc and FPdc in a grid so that each FPdc forms a raised square edge; one common version: *FPdc around the next st, dc in next 2 sts* on one row and offset on the next.
use: Thick, squishy blankets and dishcloths.
tip: Waffle fabric is narrow and dense; it may need many more stitches than plain dc.
mistake: Inserting into the top of the stitch instead of around the post, or pulling the yarn over too tight for the extra height.

name: Basketweave
how: Blocks of FPdc and BPdc (for example 4 FPdc, 4 BPdc), switching every few rows so the blocks interlock.
use: Woven-look blankets and pillows.
tip: Plan the block size into the stitch multiple.
mistake: Inserting into the top of the stitch instead of around the post, or pulling the yarn over too tight for the extra height.

name: Alpine stitch
how: Rows of sc alternate with rows that combine dc and FPdc worked around stitches two rows below; patterns define the exact sequence.
use: Textured, cable-like fabric.
tip: Always follow the stated row sequence; alpine is a family rather than one stitch.
mult: Set by the rib or cable pattern
mistake: Inserting into the top of the stitch instead of around the post, or pulling the yarn over too tight for the extra height.

name: Crocodile stitch
how: A base of V-stitches; each scale is made by working several dc down one post of the V and several dc up the other post, creating an overlapping scale.
use: Dragon-scale mitts, mermaid tails, bags.
tip: Scales overlap the row below; each row is offset by half a scale.
mult: Set by the stitch pattern; check your pattern
mistake: Losing the repeat at the row edges; count the multiple on the first row and check it every few rows.

name: Star stitch
how: A family of stitches in which loops are drawn up from several points, then all pulled through together and closed with a chain ‘eye’. Constructions vary.
use: Starry, textured fabric.
tip: Follow one pattern’s definition throughout a project.
mult: Set by the stitch pattern; check your pattern
mistake: Losing the repeat at the row edges; count the multiple on the first row and check it every few rows.

name: Solomon’s knot
how: Draw up the loop on the hook to the required length, yarn over and draw through, then insert under the single back strand of that elongated chain and work a sc to lock it.
use: Airy net-like wraps and market bags.
tip: Make every loop the same length—use a ruler or the hook shaft as a gauge.
mistake: Working into a chain stitch when the pattern means the chain space, or the reverse.

name: Loop stitch
how: Working on a wrong-side row, wrap the yarn over a finger, insert the hook and catch both strands of the wrap, draw them through, and finish as a sc so the loop is held at the back (the right side).
use: Faux fur, beards, rugs.
tip: Wrap around something of consistent size for even loops.
mult: Set by the stitch pattern; check your pattern
mistake: Losing the repeat at the row edges; count the multiple on the first row and check it every few rows.

name: Bullion stitch
how: Wrap the yarn around the hook many times (often 7–10), insert, draw up a loop, then draw it through all wraps at once (a smooth, slightly tapered hook helps), and close.
use: Roses, Irish-style motifs.
tip: Hold the wraps with a finger while drawing through.
mult: Set by the stitch pattern; check your pattern
mistake: Losing the repeat at the row edges; count the multiple on the first row and check it every few rows.

name: Tunisian simple stitch
h: One forward and one return pass
how: Forward pass: insert under the front vertical bar of the next stitch, yarn over, draw up a loop and keep it on the hook; repeat across. Return pass: yarn over, draw through 1 loop, then [yarn over, draw through 2] until 1 loop remains.
use: Woven-look fabric; base for cross-stitch embroidery.
tip: Tss curls; use a larger hook, a border, or blocking to relax it.
mult: Any number of loops (check your pattern)
mistake: Skipping the first "through 1" on the return pass, or missing the last loop at the left edge, so the piece narrows.

name: Tunisian knit stitch
how: Forward pass: insert from front to back between the front and back vertical bars of the stitch (through the fabric), draw up a loop. Return pass as usual.
use: Knit-look V-columns.
tip: Very dense and prone to curl; go up two hook sizes.
mult: Any number of loops (check your pattern)
mistake: Skipping the first "through 1" on the return pass, or missing the last loop at the left edge, so the piece narrows.

name: Tunisian purl stitch
how: Forward pass: bring the yarn to the front, insert under the front vertical bar, take the yarn back over the hook and draw up a loop. Return pass as usual.
use: Bumpy purl-like texture; ribbing with Tks.
tip: Alternating Tss and Tps (offset each row) gives the ‘honeycomb’ texture.
mult: Any number of loops (check your pattern)
mistake: Skipping the first "through 1" on the return pass, or missing the last loop at the left edge, so the piece narrows.

name: Tunisian full stitch
how: Forward pass: insert in the space between two vertical bars (through the fabric) rather than under a bar, draw up a loop; spaces shift by half a stitch each row.
use: Thick, warm fabric that curls less.
tip: Patterns specify where the first and last full stitches go—follow exactly.
mult: Any number of loops (check your pattern)
mistake: Skipping the first "through 1" on the return pass, or missing the last loop at the left edge, so the piece narrows.

name: Broomstick lace
how: Pull up a long loop from each stitch onto a large dowel or knitting needle; then work the loops off in groups (for example 5 sc through 5 loops together).
use: Airy lace wraps and blankets.
tip: Keep the loops on the dowel twisted the same way for consistent groups.
mistake: Starting a project without a practice swatch; these methods need a feel for tension first.

name: Hairpin lace
how: Wrap yarn around two prongs of a hairpin loom and work a sc spine down the center to secure each wrap; strips are then joined by their loops.
use: Lace scarves, shawls, decorative inserts.
tip: Count loops on each side of a strip—joining requires matching counts.
mistake: Starting a project without a practice swatch; these methods need a feel for tension first.

name: Corner-to-corner tile
how: A common version: ch 6, dc in 4th ch from hook and next 2 ch (first tile). Each new tile: ch 6, dc in 4th ch from hook and next 2 ch, then sl st into the ch-3 space of the previous tile, ch 3, 3 dc in the same space.
use: Pixel-picture blankets.
tip: Graph one tile = one square; decrease by sl st across the tops instead of starting a new tile.
mistake: Starting a project without a practice swatch; these methods need a feel for tension first.

name: Linked double crochet
how: Instead of a yarn over, insert the hook into the horizontal ‘bar’ halfway down the previous stitch and draw up a loop (2 loops), insert into the next stitch, draw up a loop (3 loops), [yarn over, draw through 2] twice.
use: Gap-free dc fabric for warm, wind-resistant items.
tip: The first stitch of a row links into the turning chain.
mistake: Switching between the extended and standard versions partway through, which changes the fabric height.

name: Bean stitch
how: Insert in the stitch, draw up a loop, [yarn over, insert in the same stitch, draw up a loop] 2 or more times, yarn over, draw through all loops; often followed by ch 1.
use: Small bumpy texture on hats and bags.
tip: Similar to a puff but begins with a draw-up rather than a yarn over; definitions vary.
mistake: Placing the group in the wrong stitch or space; every repeat after it shifts.

name: Ripple / chevron
how: Increases (several stitches in one) at the peaks and matching decreases (stitches worked together) at the valleys keep the stitch count constant while the rows zigzag.
use: Afghans, stripes with movement.
tip: Peak increases must equal valley decreases in every repeat or the edges will slant.
mult: Set by the stitch pattern; check your pattern
mistake: Losing the repeat at the row edges; count the multiple on the first row and check it every few rows.

name: Bruges lace tape
how: A narrow strip of a few stitches (often dc) is worked in rows, with chain loops along the edges; the tape is turned and joined to itself through those loops to form curves.
use: Flowing lace scarves, doilies and collars.
tip: Count the chain loops along each edge; joins depend on them.
mistake: Starting a project without a practice swatch; these methods need a feel for tension first.

name: Irish crochet motif
how: Motifs such as roses and leaves are worked separately, often over a padding cord, then arranged and joined with a background mesh of chains and picots.
use: Heirloom lace, collars, embellishment.
tip: Pin motifs to a fabric template before working the mesh.
mistake: Starting a project without a practice swatch; these methods need a feel for tension first.

name: Overlay mosaic
how: Rows are worked in sc (often BLO), with dc worked in front of the previous rows into a lower row to place color; each row uses one color.
use: Geometric colorwork without carried yarn.
tip: Most overlay mosaic patterns cut the yarn at the end of every row, leaving fringe.
mistake: Changing color too late: the new color must be pulled through on the last yarn over of the stitch before it.

name: Inset mosaic
how: Rows combine sc and chain-spaces; dc worked into chain-spaces of lower rows (from the right side) fill in the color pattern.
use: Reversible-looking geometric colorwork.
tip: The chart key defines which symbols mean ch-sp and which mean dropped dc—check it.
mistake: Changing color too late: the new color must be pulled through on the last yarn over of the stitch before it.

name: Front post half double crochet
how: Yarn over, insert the hook from front to back to front around the post of the stitch, yarn over, draw up a loop (3 loops), yarn over and draw through all 3.
use: Low, stretchy ribbing for hat brims and cuffs.
tip: Alternate FPhdc and BPhdc in rounds for a ribbed brim that is shorter and denser than dc ribbing.
mult: Set by the rib or cable pattern
mistake: Inserting into the top of the stitch instead of around the post, or pulling the yarn over too tight for the extra height.

name: Back post half double crochet
how: Yarn over, insert the hook from back to front to back around the post, yarn over, draw up a loop, yarn over and draw through all 3 loops.
use: Partner to FPhdc in ribbing.
tip: In rounds worked from the right side, BPhdc always looks recessed; in turned rows it looks raised on the other face.
mult: Set by the rib or cable pattern
mistake: Inserting into the top of the stitch instead of around the post, or pulling the yarn over too tight for the extra height.

name: Back post single crochet
how: Insert the hook from back to front to back around the post, draw up a loop, yarn over, draw through both loops.
use: Turning a fabric edge, outlining from behind.
tip: A round of BPsc makes a sharp fold line, handy where a band meets a body.
mult: Set by the rib or cable pattern
mistake: Inserting into the top of the stitch instead of around the post, or pulling the yarn over too tight for the extra height.

name: Back post treble crochet
how: Yarn over twice, insert around the post from the back, draw up a loop, [yarn over, draw through 2] three times.
use: Tall cables and textures worked on wrong-side rows.
tip: Pair with FPtr for deep, bold ribs.
mult: Set by the rib or cable pattern
mistake: Inserting into the top of the stitch instead of around the post, or pulling the yarn over too tight for the extra height.

name: Treble two together
how: [Yarn over twice, insert in next st, draw up a loop, (yarn over, draw through 2) twice] two times (3 loops), yarn over, draw through all 3.
use: Decreases in tall lace and fan tops.
tip: Count the loops before the final pull-through: three means the decrease is ready.
mistake: Losing track of how many stitches the decrease removes; the count should drop by exactly the number the pattern states.

name: Treble cluster
how: [Yarn over twice, insert in the same st, draw up a loop, (yarn over, draw through 2) twice] three times (4 loops), yarn over, draw through all 4.
use: Large leaf, petal and lace shapes.
tip: Patterns call these clusters, bobbles or 'leaves'; read the definition.
mistake: Placing the group in the wrong stitch or space; every repeat after it shifts.

name: Wattle stitch
how: A group of (sc, ch 1, dc) worked in one stitch, with stitches skipped between groups; on later rows each group is worked into the ch-1 space of a group below. The exact skip and edge stitches are set by the pattern.
use: Textured, slightly open blankets and wraps.
tip: Groups go into spaces, so the fabric drapes well and works up quickly.
mult: Set by the stitch pattern; check your pattern
mistake: Losing the repeat at the row edges; count the multiple on the first row and check it every few rows.

name: Sedge stitch
how: Groups of (sc, hdc, dc) worked in one stitch, skipping two stitches between groups; on later rows each group goes into the sc of a group below.
use: Bumpy, dense blankets and dishcloths.
tip: The full row instructions are in the Stitch Pattern Library.
mistake: Losing the repeat at the row edges; count the multiple on the first row and check it every few rows.

name: Trinity stitch
how: A cluster of sc worked together over three insertion points (commonly: the same stitch as the previous cluster, then the next two), closed together, followed by ch 1. Patterns vary in the insertion points.
use: Dense, knotted-look texture.
tip: Mark the stitch where each cluster begins; it is shared with the cluster before.
mult: Set by the stitch pattern; check your pattern
mistake: Losing the repeat at the row edges; count the multiple on the first row and check it every few rows.

name: Thermal stitch
how: A sc worked by inserting the hook through the back loop of the next stitch of the current row and through the front loop of the corresponding stitch in the row below, joining the two rows into one thick fabric.
use: Very warm potholders, mittens and coasters.
tip: It uses a lot of yarn and makes a firm fabric; try a hook one or two sizes larger.
mult: Set by the stitch pattern; check your pattern
mistake: Losing the repeat at the row edges; count the multiple on the first row and check it every few rows.

name: Larksfoot stitch
how: Rows alternate sc and ch-1 spaces; on the next row, a long stitch is worked over each ch-1 into the skipped stitch of the row below, usually changing color every two rows.
use: Two-color textured blankets without carried yarn.
tip: Definitions vary (some use a long dc, others a long sc); follow one pattern's rows.
mistake: Changing color too late: the new color must be pulled through on the last yarn over of the stitch before it.

name: Chain mesh
how: Loops of chains (commonly ch 5) anchored with a sc into the center of each loop on the row below.
use: Market bags, light shawls, backgrounds for appliqué.
tip: Stretchy and grows with weight; use strong cotton for bags.
mistake: Working into a chain stitch when the pattern means the chain space, or the reverse.

name: Filet mesh
how: Open squares (dc, ch 2, skip 2) and filled squares (3 dc sharing edge stitches) arranged from a chart.
use: Pictures and letters in lace.
tip: A row of n squares uses 3n + 1 stitches; see Chapter 'Lace, filet and doilies'.
mistake: Working into a chain stitch when the pattern means the chain space, or the reverse.

name: Wave stitch
how: Groups of stitches of rising and falling height (for example sc, hdc, dc, tr, dc, hdc, sc) worked along a row; the next rows fill the valleys with the opposite heights to level the work.
use: Smooth, flowing stripes without a zigzag edge.
tip: Change color for each wave and the heights do the drawing.
mult: Set by the stitch pattern; check your pattern
mistake: Losing the repeat at the row edges; count the multiple on the first row and check it every few rows.

name: Catherine wheel
how: Alternating rows of clusters (many stitches worked together) and fans (many stitches in one), offset so each fan sits over a cluster, forming wheels.
use: Bold colorwork blankets.
tip: The number of stitches gathered in each cluster must match the number in each fan, or the rows will not stay level; follow the pattern’s counts.
mult: Set by the stitch pattern; check your pattern
mistake: Losing the repeat at the row edges; count the multiple on the first row and check it every few rows.

name: Slip-stitch crochet fabric
how: Rows of slip stitches worked in the back loop only (or in both loops for a firm fabric), keeping the loops loose.
use: Ribbed hats and scarves with a knit-like elasticity; traditional in some regions as 'Bosnian' or slip-stitch crochet.
tip: Use a hook two or more sizes larger than the label; slip-stitch fabric is very tight.
mistake: Losing a stitch at the row ends: skipping the last stitch, or working into a turning chain that the pattern says does not count.

name: Tunisian extended stitch
how: Forward pass: insert as for Tss, draw up a loop, then yarn over and draw through 1 loop (a chain) and keep it on the hook. Return pass as usual.
use: Softer, drapier Tunisian fabric that curls less.
tip: A good first choice for Tunisian scarves.
mult: Any number of loops (check your pattern)
mistake: Skipping the first "through 1" on the return pass, or missing the last loop at the left edge, so the piece narrows.

name: Tunisian honeycomb
how: Alternate Tss and Tps across the forward pass, and on the next row reverse the order (Tps over Tss, Tss over Tps).
use: Reversible-looking textured fabric.
tip: Keep the edge stitches plain so the honeycomb shows cleanly.
mult: Any number of loops (check your pattern)
mistake: Skipping the first "through 1" on the return pass, or missing the last loop at the left edge, so the piece narrows.

name: Beaded single crochet
how: Thread beads onto the yarn before starting. When a bead is wanted, slide it up to the work, insert the hook, draw up a loop, and complete the sc; the bead sits on the side facing away from you.
use: Bags, bracelets, decorative edges.
tip: Beads land on the far side; plan right-side rows accordingly. Do not use beads on items for young children.
mistake: Starting a project without a practice swatch; these methods need a feel for tension first.

name: Shrimp stitch
how: Another name for reverse single crochet (crab stitch): sc worked in the opposite direction along the edge.
use: Corded edges.
tip: If a pattern says 'shrimp stitch', work crab stitch.
mistake: Working too many or too few stitches along row ends, so the edge ruffles or pulls in.

name: Corded edge (slip stitch)
how: A round of slip stitches worked evenly around an edge, keeping tension even and slightly loose.
use: Firming a stretched neckline or a wobbly border.
tip: A slip-stitch round can pull a stretched edge back in; test on part of it first.
mistake: Working too many or too few stitches along row ends, so the edge ruffles or pulls in.

name: Foundation half double crochet
how: Ch 3, yarn over, insert in 3rd ch from hook, yarn over, draw up a loop (3 loops), yarn over and draw through 1 (this is the 'chain'), yarn over and draw through all 3. For each next stitch: yarn over, insert under the two loops of the 'chain' of the previous stitch, yarn over, draw up a loop, yarn over and draw through 1, yarn over and draw through all 3.
use: Stretchy first rows for hdc hats, cowls and blankets.
tip: Count the tops, not the chain edge: each fhdc gives one stitch for the next row.
mistake: Working too tightly, so the first row will not stretch to match the fabric above it.

name: Standing double crochet
how: Make a slip knot on the hook. Hold it with a finger, yarn over, insert in the stitch or space, draw up a loop, (yarn over, draw through 2) twice.
use: Joining a new color at a granny corner or the start of a dc round without a chain or slip stitch.
tip: Hold the slip knot firmly against the hook through the first yarn over, or it rolls around the shaft.
mistake: Working too tightly, so the first row will not stretch to match the fabric above it.

name: Adjustable ring (magic ring)
h: Not a stitch; a closable center
how: Wrap the yarn into a loop with the tail crossing behind the working yarn. Insert the hook through the loop, draw up the working yarn, chain 1 to secure (this chain does not count), work the first round into the ring over both strands, then pull the tail to close the center.
use: Closed centers for amigurumi, hats worked top-down, and motifs.
tip: Weave the tail in two directions before you trust the ring; a single pass can work loose.
mistake: Weaving the tail in only one direction, so the ring opens in wear.

name: Chain ring
h: Not a stitch; a fixed center
how: Chain the number given, then slip stitch into the first chain to form a ring. Work the first round into the center of the ring, not into the chains.
use: Motifs and lace that are meant to have a small open center.
tip: If a pattern says 'ch 4, join with sl st to form a ring' and you prefer a magic ring, the center will be smaller; check that the first round still lies flat.
mistake: Working too tightly, so the first row will not stretch to match the fabric above it.

name: Stacked single crochet (chainless start)
h: About the height of a dc
how: Single crochet in the first stitch. Insert the hook under the left vertical leg of that sc, yarn over, draw up a loop, yarn over and draw through both loops. The pair stands in for the first dc.
use: Straighter row edges in dc fabric than a ch-3 turning chain gives.
tip: The stacked pair counts as the first dc of the row; work the last dc of the next row into its top.
mistake: Working too tightly, so the first row will not stretch to match the fabric above it.

name: Extended half double crochet
how: Yarn over, insert in the stitch, yarn over, draw up a loop (3 loops), yarn over and draw through 1, yarn over and draw through all 3.
use: Drapier hdc fabric; a height between hdc and dc.
tip: Definitions of extended stitches vary; follow the stitch key in your pattern.
mistake: Switching between the extended and standard versions partway through, which changes the fabric height.

name: Linked half double crochet
how: Instead of the opening yarn over, insert the hook into the horizontal bar near the middle of the previous stitch and draw up a loop, then insert in the next stitch, draw up a loop (3 loops), yarn over and draw through all 3.
use: Wind-resistant hats, bags and dense blankets.
tip: Because each stitch is attached to the one before, the fabric has very little stretch sideways.
mistake: Switching between the extended and standard versions partway through, which changes the fabric height.

name: Linked treble crochet
how: Insert the hook into the upper horizontal bar of the previous stitch and draw up a loop, insert into the lower bar and draw up a loop, insert in the next stitch and draw up a loop (4 loops), then (yarn over, draw through 2) three times.
use: Tall solid fabric where ordinary trebles would leave gaps.
tip: For the first stitch of a row, use the turning chain's chains as the 'bars'.
mistake: Switching between the extended and standard versions partway through, which changes the fabric height.

name: Working into the back bump of a chain
us: in back bump / back bar of ch
how: Turn the chain so the back faces you. Each chain has one bump; insert the hook under that bump only and work the stitch.
use: A foundation edge that looks like the V-tops of the last row, so both ends of a scarf or blanket match.
tip: Use a hook one size larger for the chain; back-bump foundations are firm.
mistake: Changing which loop or space you work into from row to row, so the texture shifts.

name: Working into a chain space
how: Insert the hook into the open space under the chain (not into the chain stitches themselves) and work the stitch around the chain.
use: Granny squares, mesh, shells and most lace.
tip: When a pattern says 'in the next ch' it means into a chain stitch; 'in the next ch-sp' means into the space. The two look different and give different counts.
mistake: Changing which loop or space you work into from row to row, so the texture shifts.

name: Working between stitches
how: Instead of inserting under the top two loops, insert into the gap between the posts of two stitches in the row below.
use: Granny stripes, some textured stitches, and offset rows that sit like bricks.
tip: Patterns that work between stitches often keep the same count by changing where the first and last stitch go; follow the edge instructions exactly.
mistake: Changing which loop or space you work into from row to row, so the texture shifts.

name: Working over a strand (encasing)
how: Lay the strand (a yarn tail, a second color or a cord) along the tops of the stitches and work each stitch around it, so the strand is hidden inside.
use: Tapestry crochet, hiding tails as you go, and adding firmness to basket edges.
tip: Tug the carried strand gently every few stitches so it neither puckers the fabric nor forms a loop.
mistake: Changing which loop or space you work into from row to row, so the texture shifts.

name: Front post double crochet two together
how: [Yarn over, insert from front to back to front around the post of the next stitch, yarn over, draw up a loop, yarn over and draw through 2] twice (3 loops), yarn over and draw through all 3.
use: Decreasing in post-stitch ribs and cables without breaking the pattern.
tip: Decrease two raised stitches together in the same column, so the rib still reads as one line.
mistake: Losing track of how many stitches the decrease removes; the count should drop by exactly the number the pattern states.

name: Front post cable (crossed post trebles)
how: Skip the next 2 stitches, FPtr around each of the next 2 stitches, then working in front of the stitches just made, FPtr around each of the 2 skipped stitches.
use: Rope cables on hats, bags and blankets.
tip: Post trebles are taller than the row; on the rows between cable rows work the stitch behind each post so the fabric lies flat.
mult: Set by the rib or cable pattern
mistake: Inserting into the top of the stitch instead of around the post, or pulling the yarn over too tight for the extra height.

name: Granny cluster
how: Work 3 dc into the same space (usually a chain space or the gap between groups below). The three stitches are separate; they are not joined at the top.
use: Granny squares, granny stripes and granny ripple.
tip: A granny 'cluster' is not the same as a closed cluster (dc3tog). Read which one the pattern means.
mult: Worked in spaces; 3 sts per group
mistake: Placing the group in the wrong stitch or space; every repeat after it shifts.

name: Filet block
how: In filet worked as dc with ch-2 spaces, a block replaces a space: work 2 dc in the ch-2 space (or in the 2 dc of a block below), then dc in the next dc.
use: Drawing the picture in filet crochet: blocks are the 'ink', spaces the background.
tip: A row of n squares has 3n + 1 stitches, whether each square is a block or a space.
mistake: Working into a chain stitch when the pattern means the chain space, or the reverse.

name: Lacet
how: Over two squares: dc, ch 3, skip 2 stitches, sc in next stitch, ch 3, skip 2 stitches, dc in next stitch. It usually sits under a bar.
use: Lacy accents in filet charts.
tip: Check the chart key: some charts use a special symbol that covers two squares.
mistake: Working into a chain stitch when the pattern means the chain space, or the reverse.

name: Filet bar
how: Over two squares (usually above a lacet): dc, ch 5, skip the lacet below, dc in the next dc.
use: Topping a lacet and making open lines in filet.
tip: The ch-5 counts as five stitches of the 3n + 1 row total.
mistake: Working into a chain stitch when the pattern means the chain space, or the reverse.

name: Invisible join
how: After the last stitch of the round, cut the yarn and pull the tail through the loop. Thread it on a tapestry needle, pass it under both loops of the first true stitch of the round, then back down through the center of the last stitch.
use: Finishing a round with no visible bump, especially on borders and motifs.
tip: The join itself makes a fake V; pull it to the same tension as the stitches around it.
mistake: Working too many or too few stitches along row ends, so the edge ruffles or pulls in.

name: Tunisian twisted simple stitch
how: On the forward pass, insert the hook from left to right under the front vertical bar (the reverse of tss), yarn over and draw up a loop. Work the return pass as usual.
use: A firmer, slightly textured Tunisian fabric.
tip: Twisting closes up the fabric; check that your gauge still matches the pattern.
mult: Any number of loops (check your pattern)
mistake: Skipping the first "through 1" on the return pass, or missing the last loop at the left edge, so the piece narrows.

name: Tunisian double stitch
how: On the forward pass, yarn over, insert under the next front vertical bar, yarn over and draw up a loop, yarn over and draw through 2 loops; one new loop stays on the hook.
use: Taller, drapier Tunisian fabric and lace.
tip: Start each Tdc row with a chain (often ch 2) so the edge is as tall as the stitches.
mult: Any number of loops (check your pattern)
mistake: Skipping the first "through 1" on the return pass, or missing the last loop at the left edge, so the piece narrows.

name: Tunisian crossed stitch
how: Skip the next vertical bar, work tss in the following bar, then work tss in the skipped bar so the two cross.
use: Woven-looking texture and simple cables in Tunisian.
tip: Work crosses in pairs and keep a single tss at each edge so the selvedge stays straight.
mult: Any number of loops (check your pattern)
mistake: Skipping the first "through 1" on the return pass, or missing the last loop at the left edge, so the piece narrows.

name: Tunisian increase
how: On the forward pass, insert the hook under the horizontal strand between two vertical bars, yarn over and draw up a loop. That adds one loop to the hook.
use: Shaping triangles, shawls and wider sections.
tip: Increase one stitch in from the edge to keep the selvedge neat.
mult: Any number of loops (check your pattern)
mistake: Skipping the first "through 1" on the return pass, or missing the last loop at the left edge, so the piece narrows.

name: Tunisian decrease
how: On the forward pass, insert the hook under the next two front vertical bars together, yarn over and draw up one loop.
use: Shaping and closing Tunisian pieces.
tip: Decreases can also be made on the return pass by drawing through 3 loops instead of 2; follow your pattern's method.
mult: Any number of loops (check your pattern)
mistake: Skipping the first "through 1" on the return pass, or missing the last loop at the left edge, so the piece narrows.

name: Tunisian return pass
how: Yarn over and draw through 1 loop, then *yarn over and draw through 2 loops; repeat from * until 1 loop remains. That loop is the first stitch of the next forward pass.
use: Every standard Tunisian row: one forward pass and one return pass make one row.
tip: The first 'draw through 1' makes the edge chain; skipping it makes the left edge tight and short.
mult: Any number of loops (check your pattern)
mistake: Skipping the first "through 1" on the return pass, or missing the last loop at the left edge, so the piece narrows.

name: Tunisian slip-stitch finish
how: On the last row, instead of a forward pass, insert under the next front vertical bar, draw up a loop and pull it straight through the loop on the hook. Repeat across.
use: A neat top edge that matches the cast-on edge of Tunisian fabric.
tip: Patterns call this a bind-off, borrowing a knitting word, but it is a crochet slip stitch.
mult: Any number of loops (check your pattern)
mistake: Skipping the first "through 1" on the return pass, or missing the last loop at the left edge, so the piece narrows.

name: Double-ended hook crochet
how: A hook with a head at each end lets you pick up loops with one color, slide the work, and work them off from the other end with a second color, so the fabric can be worked in either direction or in the round.
use: Reversible two-color Tunisian fabric and Tunisian in the round.
tip: Keep the unused color hanging at the edge where it will be picked up next.
mistake: Starting a project without a practice swatch; these methods need a feel for tension first.

name: Tapestry single crochet
how: Work sc over the color not in use, so it is carried inside the stitches. Change color by drawing the new color through the last two loops of the stitch before the new color begins.
use: Charted pictures, bags and baskets.
tip: See the Tapestry Crochet Masterclass for ways to keep the motif from slanting in rounds.
mistake: Changing color too late: the new color must be pulled through on the last yarn over of the stitch before it.

name: Intarsia crochet
how: Each color area has its own ball or bobbin. Work to the color change, change color on the last yarn over of the stitch before, drop the old color on the wrong side and leave it for the next row.
use: Large color areas, letters and pictures without carried strands.
tip: Wind small bobbins and let them hang free; untwist them at the end of each row.
mistake: Changing color too late: the new color must be pulled through on the last yarn over of the stitch before it.

name: Planned pooling
how: With a yarn that repeats its colors at regular lengths, adjust stitch count and tension so each color lands on the same place every row, making an argyle or column pattern.
use: Striking argyle patterns from variegated yarn.
tip: Works only with yarns that have a regular, short color repeat; you may need to change hook size by a fraction and loosen or tighten single stitches.
mistake: Changing color too late: the new color must be pulled through on the last yarn over of the stitch before it.

name: Interlocking crochet
how: Two colors of filet mesh are worked alternately so that the dc of each layer pass through the spaces of the other, locking them together into one reversible, two-faced fabric.
use: Reversible geometric pictures, cowls and blankets.
tip: Interlocking charts show both layers in one grid; read the key for which color forms the front squares before you start.
mistake: Changing color too late: the new color must be pulled through on the last yarn over of the stitch before it.

name: Half double crochet increase
how: Work 2 hdc in the same stitch.
use: Flat circles and hat crowns worked in hdc.
tip: Stagger hdc increases from round to round to keep a circle round.
mistake: Not counting after increase rounds, so the piece cups (too few) or ruffles (too many).

name: Double crochet increase
how: Work 2 dc in the same stitch.
use: Dc circles, crowns and shaping.
tip: Two dc in one stitch can leave a small gap; that is normal and closes up in later rounds.
mistake: Not counting after increase rounds, so the piece cups (too few) or ruffles (too many).

name: Three single crochet in one stitch
how: Work 3 sc in the same stitch, usually the center stitch of a corner.
use: Square corners on sc borders and blankets.
tip: Mark the center sc of each corner; that is where the next round's corner goes.
mistake: Not counting after increase rounds, so the piece cups (too few) or ruffles (too many).

name: Back post double crochet two together
how: [Yarn over, insert from back to front to back around the post of the next stitch, yarn over, draw up a loop, yarn over and draw through 2] twice (3 loops), yarn over and draw through all 3.
use: Decreasing in post-stitch ribbing on the recessed columns.
tip: Pair with FPdc2tog to decrease a rib without losing the column pattern.
mistake: Losing track of how many stitches the decrease removes; the count should drop by exactly the number the pattern states.

name: Half double crochet three together
how: [Yarn over, insert in next stitch, yarn over and draw up a loop] three times (7 loops), yarn over and draw through all 7.
use: Decreasing two stitches at once in hdc fabric.
tip: Pull each loop up to the same height so the decrease closes neatly.
mistake: Losing track of how many stitches the decrease removes; the count should drop by exactly the number the pattern states.

name: Double crochet four together
how: [Yarn over, insert in next stitch, draw up a loop, yarn over and draw through 2] four times (5 loops), yarn over and draw through all 5.
use: Valleys of chevrons, starbursts and lace.
tip: When the pattern works all four 'legs' into the same stitch instead, it is a cluster, not a decrease.
mistake: Losing track of how many stitches the decrease removes; the count should drop by exactly the number the pattern states.

name: Double crochet five together
how: [Yarn over, insert in next stitch, draw up a loop, yarn over and draw through 2] five times (6 loops), yarn over and draw through all 6.
use: Deep chevron valleys and fan tops.
tip: Keep the yarn overs loose; six loops on the hook need room to slide.
mistake: Losing track of how many stitches the decrease removes; the count should drop by exactly the number the pattern states.

name: Half double crochet in back loop only
how: Work an hdc, inserting the hook under the back loop only of the stitch.
use: Ribbed bands and textured hats.
tip: hdc BLO forms a ridge from the unused front loop; third-loop hdc forms a different, knit-look ridge.
mistake: Changing which loop or space you work into from row to row, so the texture shifts.

name: Double crochet in back loop only
how: Work a dc, inserting the hook under the back loop only of the stitch.
use: Softer, more flexible dc fabric with a line of ridges.
tip: Back-loop dc stretches more than both-loop dc; check gauge in the back-loop version.
mistake: Changing which loop or space you work into from row to row, so the texture shifts.

name: V-stitch with chain 2
how: Work dc, ch 2, dc all in the same stitch or space.
use: Granny-style corners, airy shawls and mesh.
tip: The ch-2 space is where the next row's stitches go; count it as a space, not two stitches.
mistake: Placing the group in the wrong stitch or space; every repeat after it shifts.

name: Treble V-stitch
how: Work tr, ch 1, tr all in the same stitch or space.
use: Tall, open lace rows.
tip: Treble Vs make deep rows; fewer rows reach the length.
mistake: Placing the group in the wrong stitch or space; every repeat after it shifts.

name: Three double crochet shell
how: Work 3 dc in the same stitch.
use: Small shells, half-shells at row ends, and edgings.
tip: A 3-dc shell at each end of a shell-stitch row is the 'half shell' that keeps the edge straight.
mistake: Placing the group in the wrong stitch or space; every repeat after it shifts.

name: Seven double crochet shell
how: Work 7 dc in the same stitch.
use: Large fans and scalloped borders.
tip: Large shells need more skipped stitches on each side; follow the pattern's multiple.
mistake: Placing the group in the wrong stitch or space; every repeat after it shifts.

name: Three double crochet bobble
how: [Yarn over, insert in stitch, draw up a loop, yarn over and draw through 2] three times in the same stitch (4 loops), yarn over and draw through all 4.
use: Small, light bobbles for baby items.
tip: A 3-dc bobble and a 3-dc cluster are made the same way; patterns name them by the effect.
mistake: Placing the group in the wrong stitch or space; every repeat after it shifts.

name: Foundation treble crochet
how: Ch 4, yarn over twice, insert in 4th ch from hook, draw up a loop, yarn over and draw through 1 (the 'chain'), then (yarn over and draw through 2) three times. For each next stitch, yarn over twice and insert in the 'chain' of the previous stitch.
use: Stretchy starts for tall lace and treble fabrics.
tip: Hold the growing foundation with your thumb on the 'chain' so you can find it.
mistake: Working too tightly, so the first row will not stretch to match the fabric above it.

name: Tunisian yarn over
how: On the forward pass, wrap the yarn over the hook to add a loop between stitches. On the return pass it is worked off like any other loop, leaving a hole.
use: Tunisian lace and eyelets.
tip: Each Tyo adds a stitch; pair it with a Tunisian decrease to keep the count.
mult: Any number of loops (check your pattern)
mistake: Skipping the first "through 1" on the return pass, or missing the last loop at the left edge, so the piece narrows.

name: Scallop edging
how: *Skip 2 stitches, 5 dc in the next stitch, skip 2 stitches, sc in the next stitch; repeat from *.
use: Blanket, cardigan and baby-item edges.
tip: The edge needs a multiple of 6 stitches; adjust the last repeat or the round before to fit.
mistake: Working too many or too few stitches along row ends, so the edge ruffles or pulls in.

name: Picot edging
how: *Sc in the next 3 stitches, ch 3, slip stitch in the base of the chain (the last sc); repeat from *.
use: Delicate edges on collars, doilies and baby items.
tip: Change the spacing (every 2, 3 or 4 sc) to make picots sparse or dense.
mistake: Working too many or too few stitches along row ends, so the edge ruffles or pulls in.

name: Ruffle edging
how: Work 3 dc (or more) in every stitch of the edge; a second round of 3 dc in every stitch makes a fuller ruffle.
use: Frilly cuffs, skirt hems and doll clothes.
tip: Ruffles use a lot of yarn: each round triples the stitch count.
mistake: Working too many or too few stitches along row ends, so the edge ruffles or pulls in.

name: Beaded chain
how: Thread the beads onto the yarn first. Slide one bead up to the hook and make a chain around it, so the bead sits in the chain.
use: Beaded necklaces, lace and edgings.
tip: Pre-string a few more beads than you need; you cannot add them later without cutting the yarn.
mistake: Starting a project without a practice swatch; these methods need a feel for tension first.

name: Stripes carried up the side
how: When stripes are an even number of rows, leave the unused color at the edge and pick it up when you need it, twisting it with the working yarn every couple of rows.
use: Striped blankets and scarves without weaving dozens of ends.
tip: Keep the carried strand loose enough that the edge does not pucker; check by stretching it gently.
mistake: Changing color too late: the new color must be pulled through on the last yarn over of the stitch before it.
